facts.text: Director David Schmoeller's first draft had a Vietnam vet running a fake POW camp in his attic. Producer Charles Band thought America wasn't ready, and suggested a Nazi instead.
Klaus Kinski (Dr. Karl Gunther) allegedly started six fistfights in the first three days of shooting, which reportedly cost the production 48 hours.
Empire boss Charles Band wanted a Nazi villain so he could cast Klaus Kinski. Director David Schmoeller's reply: "You give me Klaus Kinski, and I'll give you a Nazi."
Director David Schmoeller says Klaus Kinski objected to the words 'action' and 'cut', demanded to be filmed continuously, and refused lines he disliked.
Director David Schmoeller says his second draft was written specifically for Klaus Kinski. No other actor was ever considered for the role of Dr. Karl Gunther.
Tane McClure (Sophie), daughter of Western star Doug McClure, made her film debut here. Schmoeller kept her on set because Klaus Kinski behaved politely around her and filming went faster.
At Empire Pictures, producer Charles Band commissioned posters and title ideas first, used them to pre-sell films, and had scripts written afterward. Schmoeller says Crawlspace didn't start that way.
Klaus Kinski's birth name was Klaus Günter Karl Nakszynski, so his killer landlord character, Karl Gunther, shares his real middle names. Mondo Digital called it a strange coincidence.
Schmoeller and producer Roberto Bessi wanted to fire Klaus Kinski, but Empire Pictures boss Charles Band refused. He wanted the star's name on the poster.
Schmoeller's 1999 nine-minute short Please Kill Mr. Kinski recounts the shoot. In it he alleges a producer suggested having Kinski killed for the insurance money. Band called that story fabricated.
Lori Bancroft jokes about a vampire neighbor. Fans see a wink at Klaus Kinski's earlier turns as Dracula in Nosferatu the Vampyre (1979) and as Renfield in Count Dracula (1970).
Lori mentions 'The Exorcist' while asking about a noise. The film also nods to Peeping Tom (1960), the classic about a voyeuristic killer.
The song 'Lovers Tonight' has music by Pino Donaggio, composer of Brian De Palma's Carrie, and lyrics by director David Schmoeller himself.
During an argument over shot framing, Klaus Kinski reportedly grabbed director David Schmoeller by the lapel. Empire boss Charles Band witnessed the confrontation.
Klaus Kinski disliked his wardrobe, so he bought a whole new set of clothes, billed them to the production, and kept them.
Kinski's Nazi backstory fit his own life: he was drafted into the Wehrmacht at 16 and captured by the British on his second day of action.
Makeup apprentice John Vulich was 21 on this shoot. He later won Emmys for The X-Files, Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Babylon 5. On Kinski, he said: you can't direct him, only document him.
Makeup artist John Vulich called Klaus Kinski 'certifiably insane'. Crew reportedly panicked when Kinski was left alone with a gun.
Director David Schmoeller admits on his own commentary track that Crawlspace isn't a very good film, blaming too little time and energy spent developing the script.
The apartment sets were reused from John Carl Buechler's Troll (1986). Band had built the Rome set and wanted another film to use it, so Schmoeller quickly wrote this script.
Crawlspace was shot at the same time as Stuart Gordon's Dolls, in Charles Band's Empire Pictures Rome operation, and used the tenement set built for John Carl Buechler's Troll.
Shot in Rome from November 11, 1985 to March 1986, the film cost about $1 million. It was released by Charles Band's Empire Pictures.
Schmoeller was warned about Kinski via a Playboy interview where he ranted against directors. Kinski's previous director told Schmoeller he was wonderful. That proved wrong.
David Schmoeller's later Puppet Master began as an Empire Pictures project but ended up as the first release from Charles Band's new company, Full Moon.
Watch the vents: fans spot a fishing line pulling the trolley in the duct chase, and Lori's clothes stay oddly clean after all that crawling.
Critics were not kind: Crawlspace holds a 17% score on Rotten Tomatoes from 12 reviews, though Kinski's performance is often singled out as the saving grace.
The film includes footage from Leni Riefenstahl's 1935 Nazi propaganda film Triumph of the Will.
The original UK video release was trimmed, cutting Martha's severed tongue and a scene where Tane McClure's character has her bra cut with scissors.
TV Guide gave Crawlspace 1 star out of 4, calling it "simply ugly and disturbing." Meanwhile DVD Talk's Ian Jane called it well made and praised Klaus Kinski.
The Los Angeles Times wrote: 'You could probably spend a better 90 minutes crawling through steam tunnels.' Critic Michael Wilmington still praised Kinski and the cinematography.
Tane McClure later composed songs heard in The Terminator and married Journey's Jonathan Cain. A picture of her appears in Journey's 'Faithfully' video.
Crawlspace opened in US theaters on September 26, 1986, from Charles Band's Empire Pictures, after shooting wrapped in Rome around March of that year.
Klaus Kinski died of a heart attack five years after this film, in 1991. His ashes were scattered in the Pacific Ocean.
